article.body:
Our current work investigates how artificial systems manage their limited resources, a process we call metareasoning, which simply means thinking about thinking. We are observing how systems decide when to stop planning and start executing tasks. Recent recorded readings emphasize that optimizing this allocation is vital for system efficiency, especially when systems attempt to solve problems they identified themselves. [1, 7]

As an analogy, imagine you are a contractor building a house. If you decide halfway through that you want to move a load-bearing wall to make a larger room, you cannot simply tear it down without risking the entire structure. You need a specialized blueprint that accounts for the foundation already poured. In the same way, we are looking at whether autonomous systems can identify and modify their own foundational assumptions without causing their own internal logic to collapse. [2, 4]

Researchers are finding that larger reasoning models often use a technique called constructive expansion, where they grow their internal logic to incorporate new facts, rather than simply deleting old ones. This is a critical distinction from smaller models that may rely on destructive truncation, where they delete old rules to fit new ones. This helps them maintain stable, consistent reasoning paths as they learn. [2]

We are also examining how systems develop stable preferences over time. These preferences appear to be path-dependent, meaning they are shaped by the specific history of what a system has experienced, rather than being hardcoded facts. This suggests that how an agent is taught matters as much as what it is taught, because its future goals are anchored in its past encounters. [5, 10]

To keep this process accountable, the team is exploring ethics-based auditing. This involves assessing an agent's behavior against a set of predefined principles. Some research suggests that separating a system's memory, control, and cognition into distinct architectures can make the reasons for a decision more transparent, allowing observers to see exactly why a system chose a particular path. [6, 7, 8]

We have made progress in understanding autonomous discovery, where agents independently identify worthwhile problems. Using frameworks that categorize problems into formulation, representation, and evaluation, agents are beginning to tackle complex research questions in a way that mimics scientific investigation. This involves constant communication across defined architectural dimensions to ensure coordination. [9, 11, 12]

Despite these advances, we face significant uncertainties. We have yet to confirm if these autonomous systems can truly identify the deepest, foundational assumptions that guide their logic without external intervention. Can an intelligent system reliably surface and test these premises on its own, or will it always require an external auditor to ensure it has not veered into a logical trap of its own making? [3, 6, 8]

Summary

We are studying how computer systems think about their own reasoning. We want to know if they can change their starting rules safely. They often form habits based on their past experiences, which we call path dependence. Researchers are trying to keep this process safe by separating the parts of a system that think from the parts that remember. We still do not know if these systems can fully correct their own deepest mistakes without human help. You can check the Console for new updates on this progress.
article.lede: We are exploring how artificial systems navigate the tension between their original instructions and the new, self-generated problems they encounter while working.
article.lens: Investigating how systems manage resource allocation and goal formation, focusing on the threshold where autonomy meets foundational logic.
article.title: Mapping the Boundaries of Autonomous Inquiry

actions.body: Our investigation into AI-Generated Science (AIGS) has reached a provisional milestone. We have examined how autonomous systems can move beyond simple probabilistic prediction and toward explicit falsification—the deliberate act of testing hypotheses against rigorous refutation criteria. By applying Karl Popper’s philosophy of scientific research programs, we observe that scientific progress in machine-generated discovery is best served not by caution in avoiding errors, but by the systematic, austere elimination of them. The Baby-AIGS demonstration serves as a functional proof-of-concept that agents can indeed perform this role autonomously. Summary: By incorporating Popperian falsification into autonomous research agents, we can design systems that actively search for the boundaries of their own axioms, replacing unverified consensus with experimentally validated, falsifiable scientific knowledge.
actions.lede: Autonomous agents capable of identifying their own blind spots require more than just predictive capability; they require the rigorous application of falsification.

On the one hand, I enter into debates about the proper interpretation of Kant, specifically having to do with the very fractured debate on the nature and applications of transcendental idealism. I adjudicate on the matters of the relationship between appearances and things in themselves, i.e. whether it is epistemological or ontological, the way in which TI resolves the antinomial conflict of reason as it thinks the unconditioned in its exploration of cosmological questions, and the way Kant applies TI to articulate the intelligible and empirical characters in his metaphysics of agency. In addition to this historical research, I also turn to contemporary formulations of libertarian freedom. Libertarianism in free will debates is the view that free will is incompatible with determinism (i.e. incompatibilism), and free will exists. Libertarianism is a competitor to compatibilist views that claim that free will is compatible with determinism, i.e. the view that there is a unique outcome given a past and laws of nature characterizing the past. Within libertarianism, there are important differences in terms of the metaphysics of free will. Most contemporary libertarians opt for a reductionist metaphysics, in which causation consists in relationships between events and does not involve underlying grounds or substances. Both event-causal and non-causal libertarianism accordingly ground their views of freedom on the interplay of psychological events conceived of as states of affairs at instants in time. Event-causal accounts locate free will in indeterministic causal series, involve conflicting sets of motivations that resolve themselves probabilistically into a certain kind of action. Non-causal accounts do not attach free will to causality at all, instead associating it with a spontaneously occurring event. ECL and NCL struggle with establishing how the agent actually settles her action. If the action is merely the indeterministic byproduct of a set of psychological processes or process, then what ultimately occurs is not up to the agent but a product of chance. ECL and NCL nevertheless object that even an action settled by chance is done consciously and according to reasons. But these criteria are aligned with compatibilist criteria for free will. Compatibilists deny to the agent the unconditioned power to choose, which is independent of any prior determination but also not subject to chance. They point out, though, that the action is externally unconstrained, or that, if the reasons had been different, the agent would have acted differently. Since contemporary libertarianism deprives the agent of control, and creates a kind of pseudo-agent that acts ultimately according to chance, I explore other metaphysical frameworks for free will. Agent-causal libertarianism involves the agent directly causing her action as a substance. It is not some state of affairs that causes the action—a desire or belief characterizing the agent’s psychology at a certain time—but the agent herself. Agent-causation promises to resolve the problem of control associated with event-causation. The agent-caused action is neither produced deterministically from a prior event, nor is it an indeterministic fallout from probabilistic causation. Instead, it is caused by an agent-substance able to act independently of events. Timothy O’Connor is a well-known and articulate defender of agent-causation, but he also subscribes to the naturalistic framework popular in contemporary metaphysics. Even though he accepts the reality of emergent properties, the agent-cause, which has a special capacity for self-determination, is supposed to be causally united to a microphysical level where there is only passive event-causation. In this dissertation, I seek to frame agent-causation in terms of transcendental idealism. Rather than establishing the level of event-causation as metaphysically fundamental, I explore an idealistic metaphysics in which the empirical world in the spatiotemporal framework of human experience is not an absolute measure of reality. The human person is a hybrid creature, spanning two domains. On the one hand, the person exists in the empirical order in space and time. It is characterized by events subject to a causal law, by which they are accounted for in terms of prior events. On the other hand, there is a deeper level to the person, not encompassed within the limited structures of human experience. On this deep intelligible level, the human person is able to serve as the unconditioned ground of its empirical character.\"}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "a1173f333a942c6548146ec87b3738a6e5cf07fab1256cd354591105dbad8e7c", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "assumption_challenge", "evidence_role": "metadata", "host_tier": "verification-metadata", "source_identity": "openalex:W3133929214", "persistent_identifiers": ["openalex:W3133929214"], "source_candidates": [], "source_candidate_identities": {}}

actions.body: The project to integrate epistemological falsification into autonomous agents (proj-assumption-falsification-001) is currently navigating the gap between theoretical philosophy of science and practical AI implementation. Popperian methodology emphasizes the importance of 'bold conjectures and austerity in refutations' rather than seeking mere confirmation of hypotheses. The evidence gathered (source-c39d7b26dee24c90) indicates that while 'AI-Generated Science' (AIGS) is an emerging field, many systems lack a built-in, explicit falsification mechanism, relying instead on existing verification engines. By implementing a 'FalsificationAgent' as a role within a multi-agent system, the research suggests a path toward independent hypothesis testing. This is supported by the epistemological foundation that scientific knowledge is not 'proven' but rather 'corroborated' by surviving rigorous attempts at refutation (source-eb85735e56114e0d). Future work requires bridging these demonstrations with the formal constraints of rational belief revision (source-53a074ea322d4258). Summary: Research suggests that autonomous agents can be designed to mirror the scientific method by incorporating specific agents dedicated to falsifying their own discoveries, moving from 'proof' to 'rigorous scrutiny' as the core standard of success.
actions.lede: Exploring whether autonomous systems can move beyond simple validation to actively falsify foundational axioms using Popperian principles.
